title: "Technical Appendix: Sparse LD and CSR"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    number-sections: true
---

This appendix defines the sparse linkage disequilibrium (LD) representation
used by the current `sblr` BED-to-CSR workflow. It explains the statistical
operator represented by the disk artifact, how retained LD correlations are
combined with summary-statistic marker diagonals, and which alignment and
scaling assumptions are required for valid inference.

The sparse-LD artifact is a likelihood/operator object. It does not define the
BayesC, BayesR, BayesRC, annotation, or MAF-S prior.

Throughout the Methods documentation, mathematical cross-products are written
explicitly.

The stable high-level workflow is:

1. construct sufficient statistics from the chosen genotype/phenotype sample;
2. construct sparse LD from the compatible genotype sample and marker order;
3. retain the resulting prefix and provenance;
4. pass the updated `Glist` and sufficient statistics to the appropriate CSR
   fitter.

The current binary suffixes, integer widths, floating-point widths, metadata
keys, and upper-triangle convention are implementation details. Package
readers, writers, and fitters should be used instead of manually constructing or
editing the artifact.

## From genotype data to a sparse likelihood operator

For one trait, let

$$
y\in\mathbb R^N,
\qquad
X\in\mathbb R^{N\times M},
\qquad
b\in\mathbb R^M.
$$

The Gaussian summary-statistics likelihood depends on quantities including

$$
X^\top y,
\qquad
\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X),
\qquad
y^\top y,
$$

together with enough off-diagonal information from $X^\top X$ to update the
marker-scale residual score

$$
r
=
X^\top(y-Xb)
=
X^\top y-X^\top Xb.
$$

The sparse LD artifact supplies an approximation to the off-diagonal structure
of $X^\top X$.

In the standard BED-derived workflow, the sufficient-statistic and LD branches
must use the same underlying genotype representation:

```text
same BED source
+ same marker selection and order
+ same selected individuals
+ same allele frequencies
+ compatible genotype scaling
    -> compatible summary statistics and sparse LD
```

A typical preparation flow is:

```text
BED + phenotype
  -> make_summary_stats() -> X^T y, diag(X^T X), y^T y, N
  -> make_sparse_ld()     -> Glist$sparseLD
  -> stblr_csr(...) / stblr_csr_annot(...) / mtblr_csr(...)
```

See [Summary Statistics](summary_statistics.qmd) for the complete
cross-product derivation.

## The matrix represented by the sparse artifact

Let $x_j$ denote marker column $j$ and define its diagonal cross-product

$$
w_j
=
x_j^\top x_j.
$$

For markers $j$ and $\ell$, let

$$
\rho_{j\ell}
$$

denote their signed LD correlation.

We use $\rho$ rather than $r$ for LD correlation so that the notation cannot be
confused with the residual-score vector $r$.

The streamed writer considers eligible marker pairs according to the configured
distance rules and retains a pair only when

$$
\rho_{j\ell}^2
\ge
\texttt{r2_threshold}.
$$

The stored value is signed $\rho_{j\ell}$, not $\rho_{j\ell}^2$.

The current disk artifact stores:

- only the upper triangle, $\ell>j$;
- no explicit diagonal entries;
- an implicit diagonal correlation of one; and
- only pairs that pass every enabled distance and $r^2$ rule.

Therefore the disk artifact is a sparse correlation representation. It is not
itself the complete genotype cross-product matrix $X^\top X$.

When the CSR sampler opens the prefix, it reconstructs each retained
off-diagonal cross-product as

$$
\widetilde C_{X,j\ell}
=
\rho_{j\ell}\sqrt{w_jw_\ell},
$$

where $\widetilde C_X$ denotes the sparse approximation to $X^\top X$ used by
the CSR likelihood.

The diagonal is supplied separately:

$$
\widetilde C_{X,jj}
=
w_j.
$$

Thus, conceptually,

$$
\widetilde C_X
\approx
X^\top X.
$$

The approximation arises because unretained off-diagonal entries are treated as
zero.

## Residual-score representation under CSR

Under the complete cross-product model,

$$
r
=
X^\top y-X^\top Xb.
$$

Under the sparse CSR operator, the maintained score is instead

$$
r_{\mathrm{CSR}}
=
X^\top y-\widetilde C_Xb.
$$

For marker $j$, the partial score used in a marker update is

$$
s_j
=
[r_{\mathrm{CSR}}]_j+w_jb_j.
$$

If the marker effect changes by

$$
\Delta b_j
=
b_j^{\mathrm{new}}-b_j^{\mathrm{old}},
$$

then the diagonal residual-score entry changes by

$$
[r_{\mathrm{CSR}}]_j
\leftarrow
[r_{\mathrm{CSR}}]_j
-
w_j\Delta b_j,
$$

and each retained LD neighbor $\ell$ receives the off-diagonal update

$$
[r_{\mathrm{CSR}}]_\ell
\leftarrow
[r_{\mathrm{CSR}}]_\ell
-
\widetilde C_{X,\ell j}\Delta b_j.
$$

No update propagates through an omitted edge.

This is why sparse LD is a statistical approximation rather than merely a
compressed storage format.

## What CSR means

Compressed sparse row (CSR) format represents a sparse matrix without
allocating all $M^2$ entries.

Three arrays describe the retained upper-triangle entries:

| Array | Conceptual role |
|---|---|
| `row_ptr` | cumulative offsets delimiting each row's retained entries; length $M+1$ |
| `col_idx` | column index for every retained entry; length `nnz` |
| `values` | retained signed LD correlations; length `nnz` |

For zero-based row pointers, entries belonging to row $j$ occupy positions

$$
\texttt{row\_ptr}[j]
\quad\text{through}\quad
\texttt{row\_ptr}[j+1]-1.
$$

For example,

```text
row 0: (column 1, 0.40), (column 3, -0.20)
row 1: (column 3, 0.15)
row 2: no retained entries
row 3: no retained entries
```

corresponds conceptually to

```text
row_ptr = [0, 2, 3, 3, 3]
col_idx = [1, 3, 3]
values  = [0.40, -0.20, 0.15]
```

`row_ptr` is always a cumulative pointer array.

The `one_based` option of `sparseLD_read_CSR()` converts returned **column
indices** for convenient R inspection. It does not convert the row pointers.

## Why disk-backed sparse CSR is used

A dense $M\times M$ LD matrix requires

$$
O(M^2)
$$

storage.

This is prohibitive for genome-scale marker sets even when most retained
relationships are local or above a modest LD threshold.

Sparse CSR reduces the stored result toward

$$
O(M+\mathrm{nnz}),
$$

where `nnz` is the number of retained upper-triangle off-diagonal entries.

Disk-backed construction also allows:

- one LD artifact to be reused across multiple compatible model fits;
- large sparse arrays to remain outside ordinary R memory;
- streaming construction without returning one giant in-memory sparse object
  to R.

The lower-level writer still requires working memory for selected packed
genotypes, decoded blocks, marker diagonals, and block cross-products. Sparse
storage does not imply zero construction cost.

## Stable user-facing construction contract

The supported high-level workflow is to use `make_sparse_ld()` and let
`Glist$sparseLD` carry the resulting prefix and metadata.

A lower-level explicit call may look like:

```r
ld_prefix <- file.path(output_dir, "chr1_ld")

sparseLD_stream_CSR(
  bed_files = Glist$bedfiles[chr],
  n = Glist$n,
  cls = list(cls),
  out_prefix = ld_prefix,
  rows = NULL,
  af = list(Glist$af[[chr]][cls]),
  r2_threshold = 0.001,
  block_size = 1024,
  nthreads = 4
)
```

Stable usage expectations are:

- all files belonging to one prefix are kept together;
- `sparseLD_read_CSR()` is used for structural inspection;
- public fitters normally obtain the prefix through `Glist$sparseLD$prefix`;
- explicit `ld_prefix` remains available for lower-level workflows;
- marker/sample/scaling provenance is retained externally; and
- package functions own file naming, binary decoding, index conventions, and
  conversion to sampler structures.

Manual binary-file construction is not part of the stable user-facing
contract.

## `ld_prefix` and the current disk artifact

`ld_prefix` is a path prefix, not a single file and not an in-memory matrix.

For a prefix such as

```text
path/chr1_ld
```

the current implementation derives files similar to

```text
path/chr1_ld.row_ptr.u64.bin
path/chr1_ld.col_idx.u32.0based.bin
path/chr1_ld.values.f32.bin
path/chr1_ld.meta.txt
```

These names expose current implementation choices:

- row pointers are unsigned 64-bit integers;
- column indices are unsigned 32-bit zero-based integers;
- correlations are stored as 32-bit floating-point values;
- metadata are stored in a text file.

Metadata currently record quantities such as:

- marker count;
- `nnz`;
- triangle convention;
- diagonal convention;
- value type;
- normalization;
- threshold;
- distance limits;
- block size;
- thread count;
- used sample count.

These details support validation and reproducibility but should not be treated
as a guaranteed external binary-file API.

Treat the complete prefix as one indivisible artifact.

Do not mix files from different runs or silently overwrite a prefix when
changing marker sets, samples, allele frequencies, thresholds, or windows.

## Public construction and inspection

Use:

```r
Glist <- make_sparse_ld(...)
```

for high-level construction.

Use:

```r
ld <- sparseLD_read_CSR(Glist$sparseLD$prefix)
```

for inspection.

The fitting handoff is the written prefix, normally carried through
`Glist$sparseLD`, not an ad-hoc R list assembled from lower-level native
objects.

## Marker and sample selection

### BED sources

`bed_files`
: Paths to one or more PLINK BED files.

The associated `cls` entries define the concatenated model-marker order.

### Marker columns

`cls`
: Marker-column index vectors, one per BED source.

The order within and across these vectors becomes the CSR row and column order.

### Samples

`n`
: Number of individuals encoded by the BED source.

`rows`
: Optional positive one-based sample indices.

If `rows` is supplied, LD is constructed from that selected sample. The
sufficient statistics used with the artifact must correspond to a compatible
sample definition.

### Allele frequencies

`af`
: Optional allele frequencies aligned exactly to `cls`.

If omitted, the writer estimates allele frequencies from the selected packed
genotypes.

Supplied frequencies must be finite and lie in

$$
[0,1].
$$

Allele frequencies determine the standardized marker representation and are
therefore part of the statistical operator, not merely descriptive metadata.

### Marker positions

`pos_bp`
: Optional marker base-pair positions aligned to `cls`.

These are used only when physical-distance filtering is enabled.

## LD threshold and distance windows

Sparse-LD settings change both computational cost and the likelihood
approximation.

### Squared-correlation threshold

`r2_threshold`
: Minimum squared correlation required to retain an otherwise eligible pair.

The writer compares

$$
\rho_{j\ell}^2
$$

with the threshold but stores the signed value

$$
\rho_{j\ell}.
$$

Increasing the threshold reduces `nnz` but can remove weak LD that is
collectively relevant to conditional marker inference.

### Marker-index window

`max_distance_variants`
: Maximum difference in model-order marker indices.

Positive values restrict eligible pairs to that window. A value of zero
disables the restriction under the current implementation.

### Physical-distance window

`max_distance_bp`
: Maximum base-pair separation when `pos_bp` is supplied.

Positive values restrict eligible pairs by physical distance. A value of zero
disables this restriction.

The current implementation evaluates forward position differences, so marker
positions must be aligned and consistently ordered within the intended genomic
segments.

A pair must pass **every enabled distance rule** before its squared correlation
is tested.

Disabling both distance restrictions allows all upper-triangle pairs to be
considered and can be computationally expensive. The exported wrapper fails
closed unless full-LD construction is explicitly allowed.

## Computational settings

### Block size

`block_size`
: Number of markers decoded and compared in a working block.

Larger blocks can improve matrix-multiplication efficiency but increase working
memory through decoded genotype buffers and block cross-products.

`block_size` changes the construction strategy, not the intended statistical
retention rule.

### Threads

`nthreads`
: Requested OpenMP thread count.

This affects construction performance and potentially low-level
floating-point execution details. It is not an LD threshold or prior
parameter.

## Genotype scaling

The current sparse-LD writer constructs correlation values from
allele-frequency-standardized markers.

For genotype dosage $g_{ij}\in\{0,1,2\}$ and allele frequency $p_j$, the
standardized marker value is conceptually

$$
x_{ij}
=
\frac{
g_{ij}-2p_j
}{
\sqrt{2p_j(1-p_j)}
}.
$$

Missing genotypes are represented as zero after standardization, corresponding
to mean imputation on this scale under the supplied allele frequency.

The current writer does not expose a general `scale` switch analogous to
`bed_xtx_xty()`.

For the standard BED-to-CSR handoff, sufficient statistics should therefore use
compatible standardized marker coding:

```r
stats <- bed_xtx_xty(
  ...,
  af = af,
  scale = TRUE
)

sparseLD_stream_CSR(
  ...,
  af = list(af)
)
```

Combining `bed_xtx_xty(..., scale = FALSE)` with the current standardized
correlation writer changes the scale relationship assumed when converting

$$
\rho_{j\ell}
$$

to

$$
\rho_{j\ell}\sqrt{w_jw_\ell}.
$$

Such a combination requires explicit validation rather than being assumed
compatible.

## Streaming and block-wise construction

The writer processes selected markers through pairs of working blocks.

For each eligible block pair it:

1. decodes standardized marker values into floating-point working buffers;
2. calculates candidate block cross-products;
3. converts eligible pairs to signed correlations;
4. applies distance rules;
5. applies the $r^2$ threshold; and
6. appends retained upper-triangle indices and correlations to disk.

After each row, the cumulative retained-entry count is written to `row_ptr`.

Therefore,

$$
\texttt{row\_ptr}[M]
=
\mathrm{nnz}.
$$

Streaming avoids materializing one complete dense LD matrix or one complete
sparse result in R.

It does not eliminate all memory or runtime costs. Packed genotypes, decoded
blocks, marker diagonals, block cross-products, and the candidate block-pair
search still require resources.

## Index bases and diagonal convention

Several index conventions coexist.

1. R-facing `rows` and `cls` follow their documented one-based wrapper
   conventions.
2. On-disk `col_idx` entries are currently zero-based.
3. `sparseLD_read_CSR(prefix, one_based = TRUE)` returns one-based `col_idx`
   values for convenient R inspection.

The `one_based` argument changes only returned `col_idx`.

`row_ptr` remains a zero-based cumulative pointer array whose first value is

$$
0
$$

and whose final value is

$$
\mathrm{nnz}.
$$

The current disk artifact omits diagonal entries and reports an implicit
correlation diagonal of one.

That does **not** mean the sampler uses unit marker cross-products. The actual
marker diagonals are supplied separately as

$$
\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X).
$$

Manual insertion of diagonal entries into the sparse artifact changes the
expected contract and should be avoided.

## Marker-order invariant

Sparse arrays contain positional indices, not biological marker identifiers.

The essential invariant is that all marker-indexed objects refer to the same
ordered marker universe.

Conceptually:

```text
analysis marker IDs
    == order of X^T y
    == order of diag(X^T X)
    == rows/columns of sparse LD
    == rows of annotations
    == rows of posterior marker summaries
```

At the code level, this may be checked with objects such as:

```r
marker_id <- Glist$rsidsLD[[chr]]
cls <- match(marker_id, Glist$rsids[[chr]])

stopifnot(
  !anyNA(cls),
  identical(Glist$rsids[[chr]][cls], marker_id)
)
```

For multiple BED files, concatenating the `cls` vectors defines the CSR order.

Allele frequencies and marker positions must follow the same per-file and
concatenated order.

If annotations are used later, they must be aligned to this marker universe
before fitting.

A marker permutation can produce dimensionally valid summary statistics,
sparse LD, and posterior matrices while assigning LD or annotations to the
wrong biological markers.

Dimension checks alone cannot detect this error.

## Sample invariant

The same sample definition should underlie the genotype information used for
the summary statistics and sparse LD whenever the fitted likelihood assumes one
shared genotype sample.

If `rows` is used, it must be applied consistently.

A mismatch can change:

- allele frequencies;
- marker variances;
- LD correlations;
- $X^\top y$;
- $\operatorname{diag}(X^\top X)$.

The resulting objects can remain dimensionally compatible while describing
different statistical likelihoods.

For external-GWAS analyses using a reference LD sample, exact equality is not
possible by design. In that setting the reference-sample mismatch is an
explicit approximation and should be treated as such rather than confused with
the exact BED-derived reduction.

## Reading and validating a prefix

Use the exported reader rather than manually decoding the binary files:

```r
ld <- sparseLD_read_CSR(
  ld_prefix,
  one_based = TRUE
)

stopifnot(
  ld$nrow == length(cls),
  ld$ncol == length(cls),
  length(ld$row_ptr) == length(cls) + 1L,
  length(ld$col_idx) == length(ld$values),
  tail(ld$row_ptr, 1) == length(ld$values),
  ld$index_base == 1,
  identical(ld$diag, "implicit_1")
)
```

The current reader checks structural properties including:

- required dimensions;
- expected byte counts;
- initial/final row-pointer values;
- monotonic row pointers;
- column-index bounds;
- finite values.

Additional analysis-level checks should confirm:

1. no missing marker matches;
2. intended marker count;
3. `row_ptr` length $M+1$;
4. equal `col_idx`/`values` lengths;
5. final row pointer equals `nnz`;
6. expected returned index base;
7. understood upper-triangle and implicit-diagonal conventions;
8. finite correlations in plausible correlation bounds;
9. intended sample size, thresholds, and windows;
10. exact marker-order compatibility among sufficient statistics, annotations,
    LD, and posterior rows.

The reader cannot prove scientific provenance such as sample identity, allele
orientation, phenotype compatibility, or annotation alignment. Those must be
retained separately.

## How `stblr_csr()` consumes sparse LD

A typical public call is:

```r
fit <- stblr_csr(
  stats = stats,
  Glist = Glist,
  method = "sbayesc"
)
```

During setup, the current scalar CSR implementation:

1. validates marker dimensions and structural metadata;
2. reads the zero-based upper-triangle arrays;
3. validates row pointers, column bounds, correlations, and positive marker
   diagonal cross-products;
4. ignores explicit self-pairs if encountered;
5. reconstructs retained cross-products as

   $$
   \rho_{j\ell}\sqrt{w_jw_\ell};
   $$

6. builds a symmetric in-memory neighbor representation used by the marker
   updates.

The diagonal contribution comes from

$$
w_jb_j,
$$

while retained off-diagonal contributions use the reconstructed
$\widetilde C_{X,j\ell}$ values.

Unretained off-diagonal entries are treated as zero.

Annotation-aware scalar CSR fitters use the same sparse likelihood operator.
Their differences concern the prior, not the CSR artifact.

## Multi-trait CSR use

The current MT CSR route uses the same principle: aligned marker-trait
cross-products and marker diagonals are combined with one shared sparse-LD
representation.

Mathematically, the marker-trait quantity is

$$
X^\top Y.
$$

The present MT CSR likelihood requires shared LD scaling and matching marker
diagonal cross-products across traits. It does not infer arbitrary pairwise
sample overlap merely from the sparse-LD prefix.

Cross-trait phenotype products and overlap assumptions required for full
residual covariance are separate likelihood inputs; see
[Multi-Trait Sample Overlap](multitrait_overlap.qmd).

## Scheduled sparse marker updates

Some scalar CSR samplers can use scheduled marker updates to revisit likely
null markers less frequently and to wake retained LD neighbors after an effect
change.

Controls such as:

- `full_sweep_every`;
- `candidate_threshold`;
- `candidate_lifetime`;
- `null_skip_base`;
- `null_skip_max`; and
- LD-neighbor wake-up settings

affect the computational transition schedule.

These settings are distinct from sparse-LD construction settings.

- `r2_threshold` and distance windows determine which LD edges exist in
  $\widetilde C_X$.
- scheduling controls determine when markers and retained neighbors are
  revisited during MCMC.

The prior is not changed by selecting a scheduled path, but aggressive
scheduling can affect finite-run mixing and should be checked for sensitivity.

See [Single-trait models](../notes/single_trait_models.qmd) for the practical
controls.

## Sparse LD as a likelihood approximation

Sparse CSR replaces unretained off-diagonal cross-products with zero.

Approximation enters through:

- $r^2$ thresholding;
- marker-index windows;
- physical-distance windows;
- finite-sample LD estimation;
- allele-frequency estimation;
- missing-genotype handling;
- finite-precision correlation storage;
- sample/reference mismatch;
- genotype-scaling mismatch.

Increasing `r2_threshold` or narrowing windows usually reduces:

- `nnz`;
- disk use;
- memory;
- runtime.

But it can also remove LD required to represent the conditional marker
likelihood adequately.

There is no universal threshold that is optimal for every inferential target.

A threshold that is adequate for prediction may not be adequate for local
marker allocation or fine-mapping, where distinctions among correlated markers
are particularly important.

## Missing edges mean "not retained"

A missing CSR edge should be interpreted as

> this off-diagonal LD term is absent from the fitted sparse operator,

not as

> the two markers are known to be biologically uncorrelated.

This distinction matters when interpreting:

- posterior competition among correlated markers;
- PIP;
- component allocation;
- local credible-set post-processing.

If a regional LD matrix is reconstructed later from the **same sparse
artifact**, an omitted edge cannot be recovered simply because the region is
small.

A separate dense regional reference may contain that LD information, but it
does not retroactively alter the genomic posterior obtained under the sparse
operator.

See [Fine-Mapping and Credible Sets](fine_mapping.qmd).

## Comparison with complete BED-derived likelihood information

If BED-direct and CSR fits use:

- the same genotype source;
- the same selected individuals;
- the same marker set and order;
- compatible genotype coding;
- compatible allele frequencies;
- the same phenotype;
- the same priors and model settings; and
- sufficiently complete sparse LD,

then their likelihood information can be made closely comparable.

Exact MCMC sample equality is not generally expected because:

- CSR may omit LD edges;
- finite-precision correlations are reconstructed into cross-products;
- residual states may be maintained differently;
- update schedules may differ;
- initialization may differ;
- Monte Carlo variation remains.

Comparisons should therefore focus on quantities such as:

- posterior mean effects;
- PIP rankings;
- component probabilities;
- genomic variance;
- prediction;
- sensitivity to LD threshold/window settings.

This is an operator-reduction question, not a requirement that two independent
MCMC trajectories be identical.

## Contrast with block-eigen LD

CSR and block-eigen are separate summary-statistics likelihood operators.

CSR stores selected marker-to-marker correlations explicitly.

Block-eigen instead uses within-block spectral information.

The two approximations differ:

### CSR

- preserves retained explicit LD edges;
- removes edges through threshold/window rules;
- has no mandatory genomic block boundary apart from configured windows.

### Block eigen

- removes all cross-block LD by construction;
- can additionally filter or shrink within-block spectral modes;
- uses retained factors for the canonical current scalar low-rank route;
- uses reconstructed filtered dense blocks in the current MT route.

Therefore, a sparse CSR fit and a block-eigen fit can agree in broad prediction
while allocating local posterior marker mass differently.

See [Block-Eigen LD](block_eigen_operator.qmd).

## Reproducibility

For reproducible sparse-LD analyses, retain:

- immutable identifiers for BED/reference inputs;
- selected individuals;
- marker IDs in exact CSR order;
- `cls`;
- `rows`;
- allele frequencies;
- marker positions;
- sufficient-statistic dimensions;
- scaling convention;
- all files belonging to the sparse-LD prefix;
- construction thresholds and windows;
- writer metadata;
- package version and platform;
- prior/model settings;
- MCMC settings;
- scheduling settings;
- random seeds.

Production analyses should also assess sensitivity to LD construction choices,
especially for marker-level inference.

## Reporting recommendations

A sparse-CSR analysis should report at least:

- genotype/LD reference source;
- selected marker and sample definitions;
- allele-frequency source;
- genotype scaling;
- marker-order provenance;
- `r2_threshold`;
- marker-index and physical windows;
- `nnz` or comparable sparsity information;
- whether LD and sufficient statistics come from the same sample or from a
  reference-study combination;
- whether annotation-informed or MAF-S priors were used;
- the CSR scheduling strategy if non-default sparse scheduling was used;
- sensitivity analyses relevant to the inferential target.

These quantities define the sparse likelihood approximation sufficiently to
interpret differences among analyses.

This appendix therefore owns the statistical interpretation of sparse CSR LD:
the disk artifact stores selected signed correlations, the sampler reconstructs
retained cross-products using the aligned marker diagonals, and omitted edges
are treated as zero in the fitted likelihood operator.
